title: Earned value: what it measures
blurb: Explain planned value, earned value and actual cost, and why measuring all three together shows real progress where spend-versus-budget can't.
question: Five months into a ten-month project, a hospital's sponsor hears that £90k of the £200k budget has been spent and concludes the project is under budget. The project manager says this can't be judged without earned value. What do planned value, earned value and actual cost each measure, and why are all three needed?

teach.body: Knowing you've spent £90k by month five doesn't tell you whether that is good: how much WORK did the £90k buy? Earned value management (EVM) answers this. Formally, it is a cost control technique that integrates scope, schedule and cost by comparing the work planned, the work actually done and what it actually cost, to measure performance and forecast the outcome. Plain English: is the work where it should be, and is it costing what it should?

head: Measure
Also called
Question it answers
rows: How much work should be done by now, at budget?
How much work is actually done, at budget?
What has the work done actually cost?
What should the whole project cost?
teach.caption: PV and EV are both priced at the BUDGETED rate; only AC is real money spent.

Month 5 (illustrative): PV £100k, EV £80k, AC £90k. Spend is below plan, which looks fine. But EV sits below BOTH lines: less work done than planned (behind schedule), and that work cost more than budgeted (over budget).

teach.body: For each work package, EV is its budget multiplied by how much of it is complete. A £20k work package that is half done has earned £10k, whatever was actually spent. Because '90% done' claims are notoriously optimistic, many organisations use objective rules, such as crediting value only when a work package is finished, or at agreed milestones. EV can never exceed the BAC: once all the work is done, you have earned the whole budget.

teach.text: Exam trap: earned value is NOT the money spent. It is the BUDGETED value of the work completed. And comparing actual cost with planned value alone (spend against plan) cannot show cost performance, because it ignores how much work was actually done.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Say what EVM is: a technique that integrates scope, schedule and cost to measure performance and forecast.
Define PV (budgeted cost of work scheduled), EV (budgeted cost of work performed) and AC (actual cost of work performed).
Explain why all three are needed: spend against budget alone doesn't show how much work was achieved.
Give a benefit (early warning, objective, supports forecasting such as EAC) and a limit (needs a good baseline; ignores quality).
PV: the work that should be done by now, valued at budget.
EV: the work actually done, valued at budget.
AC: what the work done has actually cost.
Together they integrate scope, schedule and cost; spend against budget alone can mislead.
EVM needs a WBS, a time-phased baseline, objective progress measures and actuals coded to the same structure.

summary: You can now explain what planned value, earned value and actual cost each measure and why EVM needs all three to integrate scope, schedule and cost. You can also explain what EVM needs in place, its benefits and limits, and how it adapts to iterative delivery.

A.q: Which of the following best describes earned value (EV)?
options: The actual money spent on the work so far
The budgeted cost of the work actually done
The budgeted cost of the work scheduled to date
The total approved budget for the project
A.why: EV is the budgeted cost of work performed: the value, at budget rates, of the work actually completed.

whyNot.0: Money actually spent is the actual cost (AC).
whyNot.2: The budgeted cost of work scheduled is the planned value (PV).
whyNot.3: The total approved budget is the budget at completion (BAC).

A.q: Why is earned value management said to INTEGRATE scope, schedule and cost?
options: It replaces the schedule with one budget
It reports cost and time in separate reports
It links work done to plan and to spend
It removes the need for a WBS or a CBS
A.why: EV measures work achieved (scope), compares it with the work planned by now (schedule) and with what it cost (cost), giving one combined view.

whyNot.0: EVM relies on the schedule; it doesn't replace it.
whyNot.1: Its value is in combining the measures, not reporting them separately.
whyNot.3: EVM depends on a WBS and cost coding; it can't work without them.

A.q: Planned value (PV) at a status date represents…
options: the budgeted cost of work due to be done by then
the real cost of the work done up to that date
the forecast of the project's final total cost
the cost of work still remaining after that date
A.why: PV is the budgeted cost of work scheduled: the slice of the time-phased budget for the work planned up to that date.

whyNot.1: The real cost of work done is the actual cost (AC).
whyNot.2: A forecast of final cost is the estimate at completion (EAC).
whyNot.3: The cost of remaining work is the estimate to complete, a forecast, not PV.

B.q: Halfway through a project, a director notes that only 45% of the budget has been spent and says the project must be under budget. Why can't this conclusion be drawn?
options: Spend should be compared with the risk register
It ignores how much work has been completed
Under budget can only be judged at closure
The figure should include management reserve
B.why: Spend against plan ignores achievement. If much less than half the work is done, 45% spent could mean overspending on the work achieved. EV is needed to judge cost performance.

whyNot.0: The risk register records risks; it isn't the measure for judging cost performance.
whyNot.2: Cost performance can be judged at any status date using EV and AC; that is the point of EVM.
whyNot.3: Management reserve sits outside the cost baseline and doesn't fix the missing measure of work done.

B.q: Which of the following must be in place before earned value can be measured?
options: A completed lessons learned report
A signed final account with suppliers
A time-phased baseline budget
An agreed benefits realisation review
B.why: PV comes from the time-phased baseline budget, and EV is measured against the budgets of the work packages in it. Without a baseline there is nothing to earn against.

whyNot.0: Lessons learned are captured during and at the end of the project; EVM doesn't need a completed report.
whyNot.1: A final account is settled at closure, long after EVM is in use.
whyNot.3: Benefits reviews happen after delivery and are separate from EVM.

B.q: Team leads keep reporting work packages as '90% complete' for weeks on end. What is the BEST way to make earned value more reliable?
options: Use the actual cost as the measure of progress
Ask for progress reports less often than before
Base progress on the planned value for the date
Agree objective rules for crediting work done
B.why: Objective rules, such as crediting value only when a work package is finished or at agreed milestones, stop optimistic estimates inflating EV.

whyNot.0: Spending money doesn't prove work is done; using AC as progress hides overspends.
whyNot.1: Reporting less often delays warnings without fixing the optimism.
whyNot.2: Using PV as progress would assume everything is on plan, which defeats the purpose.

C.q: Which of the following does earned value management NOT tell the project manager directly?
options: Whether the work is behind or ahead of plan
Whether the work done cost more than budget
Whether the deliverables meet quality criteria
A trend that supports a forecast of final cost
C.why: EVM measures progress and cost against the baseline. It says nothing about whether outputs meet their quality or acceptance criteria, which needs quality control.

whyNot.0: Comparing EV with PV shows schedule performance.
whyNot.1: Comparing EV with AC shows cost performance.
whyNot.3: EVM trends are used to forecast, for example the estimate at completion.

C.q: An agile team delivers in two-week time boxes with a prioritised backlog. How is value MOST sensibly earned on this project?
options: When backlog items are done and accepted
When the team's hours are booked each day
When the sponsor approves the business case
When each time box's budget has been spent
C.why: In iterative delivery, value is earned when features are completed to the agreed definition and accepted, often shown on a burn-up chart against the planned features.

whyNot.1: Booking hours records cost (AC), not work achieved.
whyNot.2: Approving the business case authorises the project; it doesn't earn value.
whyNot.3: Spending a time box's budget is cost, not proof that anything useful was delivered.

C.q: Which THREE are benefits of earned value management? 1: Early warning of cost and schedule trends. 2: An objective, integrated view of progress. 3: It removes the need for risk management. 4: A basis for forecasting the final cost.
options: 1, 2 and 3
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
1, 2 and 4
C.why: EVM gives early warning, an objective integrated view and the trends used to forecast final cost. It does not replace risk management.

whyNot.0: Statement 3 is wrong: EVM complements risk management; it doesn't replace it.
whyNot.1: Statement 3 is wrong, and this leaves out the integrated view (2).
whyNot.2: Statement 3 is wrong, and this leaves out early warning (1).

reteach.title: Painting a house
reteach.question: You pay a decorator £1,000 to paint ten rooms over ten days (£100 a room). After five days, what do you need to know to judge how it's going?

blocks.h: Rooms planned, rooms painted, money paid
blocks.body: By day five you PLANNED five rooms: £500 of the job (planned value). The decorator has actually PAINTED four rooms, worth £400 at the agreed £100 a room (earned value). You've PAID £600 for those four rooms because of extra paint and hours (actual cost). Paid versus plan (£600 versus £500) only says you've spent more. Adding rooms painted shows the full picture: behind (4 not 5) and over cost (£600 for £400 of work).

blocks.h: The decorating job, day by day
blocks.caption: Day five: £500 planned, £400 of rooms painted, £600 paid.

blocks.text: The rooms painted (EV) are valued at the agreed price per room, not at what you paid. That's what makes EV a fair yardstick.

explain.body: PV is the budgeted cost of work scheduled: how much of the time-phased budget should have been 'used up' by the work planned to date. Over the whole project it traces the baseline S-curve and ends at the BAC.

test.q: Where does the planned value at any date come from?
options: The supplier's latest invoices
The time-phased baseline budget
The team's progress estimates
The finance team's cash balance
test.why: PV is read from the time-phased baseline: the budgeted cost of the work scheduled up to that date.

whyNot.3: A cash balance is not a measure of planned work.

explain.body: EV is the budgeted cost of work performed. For each work package, multiply its budget by the proportion complete, using objective rules. It measures achievement in money terms, at budget rates.

test.q: A work package is exactly half complete, but it has already cost more than half of its budget. What does its earned value reflect?
options: The amount actually spent so far
Its whole budget, once started
Nothing until it is finished
Half of its budget, at budget rates
test.why: EV is budget multiplied by the proportion complete, so half the work earns half the budget, whatever was spent. (Some organisations agree stricter crediting rules, but the principle is budget × progress.)

whyNot.0: The amount spent is the actual cost, not the value earned.
whyNot.1: The whole budget is earned only when the work package is complete.
whyNot.2: Value is earned as work progresses unless a stricter rule has been agreed.

explain.body: AC is the actual cost of work performed: the real money incurred for the work done to date, booked against the same cost codes as the budget so it can be compared like for like with EV.

test.q: Why must actual costs be booked to the same cost codes as the budget?
options: So suppliers are paid more quickly
So they compare like for like with EV
So the team can claim more overtime
So the schedule float is increased
test.why: Coding actuals to the same structure as the budget lets AC be compared with EV for the same work, revealing true cost performance.

whyNot.0: Payment speed is a finance process unrelated to EVM comparisons.
whyNot.2: Cost coding has nothing to do with overtime entitlement.
whyNot.3: Float is a schedule property, unaffected by cost coding.

explain.body: PV versus EV shows schedule performance (is the work where it should be?). EV versus AC shows cost performance (did the work cost what it should?). Using just two of the three, such as spend against plan, misses one of these questions.

test.q: Which pair of measures shows whether the work done has cost more or less than budgeted?
options: EV and AC
PV and AC
PV and EV
BAC and PV
test.why: Comparing EV (budgeted value of work done) with AC (what it actually cost) shows cost performance.

whyNot.1: PV and AC compares spend with plan, which ignores how much work was done.
whyNot.2: PV and EV shows schedule performance, not cost.
whyNot.3: BAC and PV are both from the baseline; neither measures actual progress or spend.
